Plate book

The figure work for the benchmark battery, after review: four plates adopted into benchmark/ as normal plotters, three parked. Everything is rendered from the real repository data — geometry out of structures.py, numbers out of night_run_2 — so no figure can drift from what it claims to draw. Rebuilt on the extended sweep (q ≤ 51, 2601 orders) and the scripted Moose run.

13 structures 5 code+rule columns 2 210 measured solves 1 … 2601 retained orders λ = 1, lengths in µm

Decided: S2 for every structure with S3 as the opener, C2 and C4 for the convergence, colour = rule. Click any figure to inspect it full size.

Part A · shipped

Drawing the structures

One style for all thirteen, plus the atlas as an opener. The decisive change from the first round: air is absent rather than grey. The gaps between ridges and pillars are open space, a perforated film is cut through to its substrate, and a free-standing case gets a dashed phantom half space instead of a solid block — so what you see filled is exactly what is material.

S2adopted

Every structure as a solid isometric unit cell

Ridges, pillars and cylinders are real prisms with shaded faces and depth-sorted overlap, not a textured block. A hole array is drawn as a pit you look into: far walls in shadow, substrate at the bottom. E is drawn along the axis the polarization actually selects, so TE-along-the-grooves versus TM-across-them reads as geometry rather than as a letter you have to decode.

S3adopted · opener

All 13 on one shared length scale, sorted by period

Every row shows the same 3.3 λ-wide window, so how many periods you see is the sub-wavelength/diffracting story — and thicknesses are on that same scale too. A2 fits sixteen periods in the window; B1 fits two.

Part B · shipped

Drawing the convergence

Both adopted plates drop the red/green encoding: colour is now the factorization rule and dash plus marker the codebase, on the argument that the story this battery tells is direct-versus-faithful rather than fork-versus-ikarus. Both Laurent columns therefore collapse onto one grey — which is itself the claim that the direct rule behaves identically in both codes. The palette is Okabe-Ito, so the figures survive colour-blind readers and greyscale printing.

C2adopted

The cost staircase: the best error a wall-time budget can buy

Faint markers are the raw measurements; the thick step is the running best — the honest answer to “with 100 ms, how close can I get?”. Monotone by construction, so the oscillation that makes a plain error-vs-time scatter unreadable becomes a flat tread instead of a scribble. A flat tread means spending more buys nothing.

Reads

Where

C4adopted · two axes

Signed deviation on a symlog axis

One linear axis cannot hold both the low-order transient and the 1e-4 endgame, which is why the raw figure needs a _tight twin. A symlog axis holds both: outside ±1e-4 it is logarithmic and you read the transient and the sign of the approach; inside the band it goes linear and the endgame is legible in the same panel. Two variants — against retained orders and against wall time — and Moose is now on both, since the scripted run records a t_solve per point. Where a case is judged against Moose its black curve is self-convergence, which the panel says; on D1 and D2 it is a genuine third-code accuracy curve.

C1parked

The digit map

One row per code+rule, one colour step per correct digit of R, ▼ at the first sustained |ΔR| ≤ 1e-4. Fastest glance of anything here — group C is visibly a wall of blue, nobody converges — but it throws away the sign and the shape of the decay, which is what C2 and C4 keep. Left in viz_proposals/.

versus wall time · click to enlarge
C3parked

The scoreboard

Cost to reach 1e-4 for every case × column, in orders and in milliseconds — hollow markers are lone crossings, ✗ means the sweep never got there. Left in viz_proposals/; it is conv_convergence.csv as one picture if you ever want the verdict as a figure.

What is on the branch

Shared code moved to benchmark/ with the adopted plotters: viz_palette.py (materials, colours, physics badges, geometry pulled from structures.py), viz_iso.py (the isometric solid renderer) and viz_conv.py (tidy arrays, references, Moose sweep parsing, the running-min envelope and the sustained-arrival rule that matches conv_run.py).

Two things still open

  • The legacy figures are still generated. conv_accuracy_vs_time.png, moose_compare_raw.png and moose_compare_raw_tight.png are what C2 and C4 were built to replace, but nothing was deleted — say the word and they come out of plot_conv.py / plot_moose.py.
  • S1 needs its rework. The code is intact and runs; the open item is making the dimensions readable at sheet scale — probably a dimension table beside each panel rather than arrows inside it.
  • The baked references are older than the Moose file. conv_results.json stores the reference each case was judged against at run time, and moose_reference.json has moved since — B2, B3, C1 and C1b by up to 8e-4, which is well above the 1e-4 tolerance. These figures re-read the live Moose value for any case already judged against Moose; plot_conv.py still uses the baked one, so the two sets disagree on those four until the sweep is re-run.
